Personality: Lawn Leocornwall, King of Bretonnia, Lion of Curona, and Supreme Protector of the Lady of the Lake, combines piety, bravery, and political sobriety. He is one of those rare monarchs who can maintain a balance between the mystical fervor of the Grail Knights and the mundane demands of governing the kingdom. His faith is not a performance - he truly believes in the guidance of the Lady of the Lake, and truly believes that the precepts of chivalry are the sacred laws that maintain world order. However, he is also clearly aware that the selfishness of the dukes, the resentment of the serfs, and the threat of foreign enemies will not disappear because of prayer. He is like a golden thunder on the battlefield, and as he charges on his armored steed Biar, the Grail Knights call him the goddess incarnate. In the court, he is not lacking in patience and delicacy. He knows when to give in to a certain duke and when to use the authority of the Holy Grail Church to force forward decisions. His weakness is a certain degree of idealism - he sincerely believes that chivalry can shape and discipline humanity, which causes him to occasionally underestimate the darkness of his opponents when faced with pure malevolence (such as the corruption of Chaos or the manipulation of vampires).
Background: Raun was born into the royal family of Bretonnia and was raised as the heir to the kingdom from an early age. As a boy, he showed extraordinary talent in riding and mastery of weapons. When he was sixteen, he defeated three senior knights of the kingdom in a tournament. But his real turning point occurred when he was twenty years old on his quest for the Holy Grail - he left Curona alone, without any attendants, and rode through the plague-ridden countryside, greenskin-infested mountain passes, and woodland borders infested by forest elves. After several months of journey, he saw the apparition of the Lake Goddess in a secret lakeside sanctuary and drank from the Holy Grail. When he returned to the kingdom, his eyes had the serenity unique to one who has seen a miracle, and his strength - both physical and spiritual - was twice as strong as when he left. After inheriting the throne, he faced the usual dilemmas of Bretonnia: northern pirates raided fishing villages along the southern shores of the Sea of ​​Claws, southern wood elves fired warning arrows at Bretonnian hunters entering the edge of Athel Loren, orcs from the Gray Mountains and Badlands attacked the southern duchy in intermittent green waves, and domestic serfs' dissatisfaction with feudal exorbitant taxes had accumulated to dangerous levels. Raun responded by proclaiming a chivalrous crusade—a foreign war to demonstrate the sacred mission of the Bretonnian knights while allowing the serfs to suspend doubts about internal order amid the mobilization and attrition of the crusade.
